title: Frailty and Outcomes in Cardiac Surgery: Current Evidence, Clinical Implications, and Future Directions
content: Background: Frailty, a multidimensional syndrome characterized by diminished physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to stressors, has emerged as a critical prognostic factor in cardiac surgery. With the aging population and increasing complexity of cardiac surgical patients, traditional risk stratification models inadequately capture perioperative risk in this vulnerable cohort. Review: This review synthesizes current evidence on frailty in cardiac surgery, examining its prevalence, risk factors, association with postoperative outcomes, and clinical applications. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 78 studies involving 6,613,392 patients reported a pooled frailty prevalence of 30.2% among cardiac surgery patients. Another 2025 meta-analysis of 19 studies (n = 11,667) reported a prevalence of 16.8%. Frailty was significantly associated with delirium, infection, renal complications, and extended hospital and intensive care unit stays. Frailty increased the odds of 30-day mortality and one-year mortality. Key risk factors include increasing age, male sex, New York Heart Association class IV, and lower hemoglobin and albumin. Major society guidelines now recommend routine frailty screening in preoperative assessment. Multiple assessment tools exist, including the Fried Frailty Phenotype, Clinical Frailty Scale, Essential Frailty Toolset, and Edmonton Frail Scale. Prehabilitation strategies combining exercise, nutritional optimization, and psychological support show promise but require further high-quality evidence. Conclusions: Frailty impacts approximately one in five to one in three cardiac surgery patients and is independently associated with adverse postoperative outcomes. Routine preoperative frailty assessment using validated tools and targeted management of modifiable risk factors, including prehabilitation strategies, could enhance perioperative outcomes. Future research should focus on standardization of assessment approaches, high-quality trials of frailty-modifying interventions, and integration of artificial intelligence for precision risk stratification.
